paragraphs: MADISON, with HAMILTON

Among the confederacies of antiquity, the most considerable was that of the Grecian republics, associated under the Amphictyonic Council. By the best accounts handed down about this celebrated institution, it bore a very instructive resemblance to the present Confederation of the American States.

The members kept the character of independent and sovereign states, and had equal votes in the federal council. This council had general authority to propose and decide whatever it judged necessary for the common welfare of Greece; to declare and carry on war; to decide, in the last resort, all controversies between the members; to fine the aggressing party; to use the whole force of the confederacy against the disobedient; and to admit new members. The Amphictyons were the guardians of religion and of the immense riches belonging to the temple of Delphos, where they had the right of jurisdiction in controversies between the inhabitants and those who came to consult the oracle. As a further provision for the effectiveness of the federal powers, they took an oath to defend and protect the united cities mutually, to punish those who violated this oath, and to take vengeance on sacrilegious despoilers of the temple.

In theory, and on paper, this apparatus of powers seems amply sufficient for all general purposes. In several important respects it exceeds the powers listed in the Articles of Confederation. The Amphictyons had in their hands the superstition of the times, one of the principal engines by which government was then maintained. They had a declared authority to use coercion against refractory cities, and were bound by oath to exert this authority on the necessary occasions.

The experiment, nevertheless, was very different from the theory. The powers, like those of the present Congress, were administered by deputies appointed wholly by the cities in their political capacities, and were exercised over those cities in the same capacities. Hence came the weakness, the disorders, and finally the destruction of the confederacy. The more powerful members, instead of being kept in awe and subordination, tyrannized successively over all the rest. Athens, as we learn from Demosthenes, was the arbiter of Greece for seventy-three years. The Lacedaemonians governed it next, for twenty-nine years. At a later period, after the battle of Leuctra, the Thebans had their turn at domination.
According to Plutarch, it happened all too often that the deputies of the strongest cities overawed and corrupted those of the weaker, and that judgment went in favor of the most powerful party.

Even in the midst of defensive and dangerous wars with Persia and Macedon, the members never acted in concert, and some or other of them were always the dupes or the hirelings of the common enemy. The intervals of foreign war were filled up by domestic upheavals, convulsions, and carnage.

After the conclusion of the war with Xerxes, it appears that the Lacedaemonians demanded that a number of the cities be expelled from the confederacy for the unfaithful part they had played. The Athenians saw that the Lacedaemonians would lose fewer partisans by such a measure than they themselves would, and that the Lacedaemonians would become masters of the public deliberations. They therefore opposed the attempt vigorously and defeated it. This piece of history proves at once the ineffectiveness of the union, the ambition and jealousy of its most powerful members, and the dependent and degraded condition of the rest. The smaller members, though entitled by the theory of their system to revolve in equal pride and majesty around the common center, had in fact become satellites of the orbs of primary magnitude.

The Abbe Milot says that if the Greeks had been as wise as they were courageous, experience would have warned them of the need for a closer union. They would have used the peace that followed their success against the Persian arms to bring about such a reform. Instead of this obvious policy, Athens and Sparta, swollen with the victories and the glory they had won, became first rivals and then enemies, and did each other infinitely more harm than they had suffered from Xerxes. Their mutual jealousies, fears, hatreds, and injuries ended in the celebrated Peloponnesian war, which itself ended in the ruin and slavery of the Athenians who had begun it.

As a weak government, when not at war, is always agitated by internal dissensions, so these never fail to bring on fresh calamities from abroad. The Phocians had plowed up some consecrated ground belonging to the temple of Apollo, and the Amphictyonic Council, according to the superstition of the age, imposed a fine on the sacrilegious offenders. The Phocians, backed by Athens and Sparta, refused to submit to the decree. The Thebans, with some of the other cities, undertook to uphold the authority of the Amphictyons and to avenge the violated god. The Thebans, being the weaker party, invited the assistance of Philip of Macedon, who had secretly encouraged the quarrel. Philip gladly seized the opportunity of carrying out the designs he had long planned against the liberties of Greece. By his intrigues and bribes he won over to his interests the popular leaders of several cities. By their influence and votes he gained admission into the Amphictyonic Council. And by his arts and his arms he made himself master of the confederacy.

Such were the consequences of the fallacious principle on which this interesting establishment was founded. A judicious observer, writing on the fate of Greece, says that if she had been united by a stricter confederation and had persevered in her union, she would never have worn the chains of Macedon, and might have proved a barrier to the vast projects of Rome.
The Achaean league, as it is called, was another society of Grecian republics, and it gives us valuable instruction.

The union here was far more intimate, and its organization much wiser, than in the preceding instance. It will accordingly appear that, though the league did not escape a similar catastrophe, it by no means deserved it equally.

The cities composing this league kept their municipal jurisdiction, appointed their own officers, and enjoyed perfect equality. The senate, in which they were represented, had the sole and exclusive right of peace and war; of sending and receiving ambassadors; of entering into treaties and alliances; and of appointing a chief executive, or praetor as he was called. The praetor commanded their armies. With the advice and consent of ten of the senators, he not only administered the government while the senate was not in session but also had a great share in its deliberations when it was assembled. According to the original constitution, two praetors were associated in the administration, but on trial a single one was preferred.

It appears that the cities all had the same laws and customs, the same weights and measures, and the same money. But how far this result came from the authority of the federal council is left uncertain. It is said only that the cities were in a manner compelled to accept the same laws and usages. When Lacedaemon was brought into the league by Philopoemen, it was accompanied by the abolition of the institutions and laws of Lycurgus and the adoption of those of the Achaeans. The Amphictyonic confederacy, of which she had been a member, had left her in the full exercise of her government and her legislation. This circumstance alone proves a very important difference in the character of the two systems.

It is much to be regretted that such imperfect records remain of this curious political structure. If its internal structure and regular operation could be ascertained, it would probably throw more light on the science of federal government than any of the similar experiments we know of.

One important fact seems to be attested by all the historians who take notice of Achaean affairs. It is that, both after the renewal of the league by Aratus and before its dissolution by the arts of Macedon, there was infinitely more moderation and justice in the administration of its government, and less violence and sedition among the people, than were to be found in any of the cities that exercised SINGLY all the prerogatives of sovereignty. The Abbe Mably, in his observations on Greece, says that the popular government, which was so tempestuous elsewhere, caused no disorders among the members of the Achaean republic, BECAUSE IT WAS THERE TEMPERED BY THE GENERAL AUTHORITY AND LAWS OF THE CONFEDERACY.

We are not to conclude too hastily, however, that faction did not, to a certain degree, agitate the particular cities, much less that due subordination and harmony reigned in the general system. The contrary is sufficiently shown by the ups and downs and the fate of the republic.

As long as the Amphictyonic confederacy lasted, that of the Achaeans, which included only the less important cities, made little figure on the stage of Greece. When the former fell victim to Macedon, the latter was spared by the policy of Philip and Alexander. Under the successors of these princes, however, a different policy prevailed. The arts of division were practiced among the Achaeans. Each city was seduced into a separate interest, and the union was dissolved. Some of the cities fell under the tyranny of Macedonian garrisons, others under that of usurpers springing out of their own confusion. Shame and oppression soon awakened their love of liberty. A few cities reunited. Others followed their example as opportunities were found of getting rid of their tyrants. The league soon embraced almost the whole Peloponnesus. Macedon saw its progress but was kept by internal dissensions from stopping it. All Greece caught the enthusiasm and seemed ready to unite in one confederacy, when the jealousy and envy of Sparta and Athens at the rising glory of the Achaeans threw a fatal damper on the enterprise. Dread of the Macedonian power led the league to court the alliance of the Kings of Egypt and Syria, who, as successors of Alexander, were rivals of the king of Macedon. This policy was defeated by Cleomenes, king of Sparta. His ambition led him to make an unprovoked attack on his neighbors, the Achaeans, and as an enemy of Macedon he had enough influence with the Egyptian and Syrian princes to bring about a breach of their engagements with the league.

The Achaeans were now reduced to the dilemma of submitting to Cleomenes or of begging the aid of Macedon, their former oppressor. They adopted the latter expedient. The contests of the Greeks always gave that powerful neighbor a pleasing opportunity to meddle in their affairs. A Macedonian army quickly appeared. Cleomenes was defeated. The Achaeans soon found, as often happens, that a victorious and powerful ally is only another name for a master. All that their most abject compliance could obtain from him was toleration of the exercise of their laws. Philip, who was now on the throne of Macedon, soon provoked fresh combinations among the Greeks by his tyrannies. The Achaeans, though weakened by internal dissensions and by the revolt of Messene, one of their members, joined the AEtolians and Athenians and raised the standard of opposition. Finding themselves, even with this support, unequal to the undertaking, they once more had recourse to the dangerous expedient of bringing in foreign arms. The Romans, to whom the invitation was made, eagerly accepted it. Philip was conquered; Macedon was subdued. A new crisis followed for the league. Dissensions broke out among its members. The Romans encouraged them. Callicrates and other popular leaders became mercenary instruments for luring their countrymen astray. To nourish discord and disorder more effectively, the Romans had already proclaimed universal liberty(1) throughout Greece, to the astonishment of those who trusted in their sincerity. With the same insidious aims, they now seduced the members from the league by appealing to their pride about the violation it committed on their sovereignty. By these arts this union, the last hope of Greece, the last hope of ancient liberty, was torn to pieces. Such weakness and distraction were introduced that the arms of Rome found little difficulty in completing the ruin their arts had begun. The Achaeans were cut to pieces, and Achaia was loaded with chains, under which it groans to this hour.

I have thought it not superfluous to give the outlines of this important portion of history, both because it teaches more than one lesson and because, as a supplement to the outline of the Achaean constitution, it emphatically illustrates the tendency of federal bodies toward anarchy among the members rather than toward tyranny in the head.
1. This was only a more plausible-sounding name for the independence of the members from the federal head.
